en: Bāṇa: *Harṣacarita*, Chapter Five.
Fate, having first ordained happiness for men and subsequently a terrible suffering, makes the world tremble like lightning and then strikes it down with a thunderbolt. (BaHcar_5.1)
Time alone, as it revolves, single-mindedly and with utter disregard casts down many great men alike, like an infinite mountain casting down rocks. (BaHcar 5.2)

Then once, the king summoned Rājyavardhana, clad in armor, and dispatched him to the North with a vast following of ancient ministers and loyal great vassals to slay the Hūṇas, as a lion goes forth against deer, accompanied by a prince of lions endowed with immeasurable strength.
And as he was departing, King Harṣa followed him for several stages by means of his horses.

Once his brother had entered the quarter resplendent with the luster of Kailāsa, the king—still in the prime of youth and impelled by the passion for valor—roamed the slopes of the snowy mountains, which abound in lions, śarabhas, tigers, and boars; there, the radiance of his body was touched by the rays of the longing glances of the forest deities.
Sporting in the hunt, the deer-eyed prince remained outside for several days.
And by discharging brilliant arrows from his bow drawn back to his ear, he rendered the forests devoid of wild beasts in a very few days.

One day, however, toward the fourth watch of the night, at the break of dawn, he saw in a dream a lion being consumed by an irresistible forest fire that turned all the quarters of the sky tawny with its flickering masses of flames.
And in that very forest fire, he saw a lioness who, having abandoned her cubs, was leaping up and throwing herself down.
The thought occurred to him: "In this world, the bonds of affection composed of love are indeed harder than iron, since even animals behave in such a way when drawn by them.
As he reflected on this, his right eye throbbed again and again.
A trembling suddenly spread through his limbs; for no apparent reason, his heart seemed to move from its place within his chest,
and for no cause whatsoever, a profound sense of unease arose.
"What is this?"— with his mind thus agitated by various doubts that had arisen, his fortitude gone, and his face bowed down with anxiety,
the partridge-eyed prince for a moment made the earth appear like a grove of land-lotuses with his eyes whose pupils were fixed in a stare.
And during that day, he pursued the hunt with a truly desolate heart.

As the sun ascended toward midday, he returned to his quarters and remained there full of apprehension, reclining upon a cane couch spread over the floor with a white silken pillow; his slender body was being gently fanned on both sides by attendants, and his frame was anointed with drops of exceedingly cool sandalwood paste.

Then, from afar, he was seen with his shaven head adorned by a ragged tunic of dark-blue hue, its interior filled with a letter; his body bore a pallor imposed by fatigue and the sun, as if being reduced to charcoal by the fire of internal grief; he was followed, as it were, by the Earth herself—curious to hear news of the king—under the guise of a column of dust raised by his exceedingly rapid steps in his great haste; and both his sides were fanned by the edges of his wide upper garment, which fluttered in the wind blowing toward him.
He seemed to have suddenly grown wings through his extreme haste as he sped along; he was being driven from behind by the command of his master and pulled from the front by it;

with long exhalations of laborious breath, a reflection formed upon the surface of his perspiring forehead made him appear as if his letter were being carried away by the sun out of curiosity for the task;
and his body was rendered vacant by his senses, as if they had fallen away in agitation, because of the gravity of the purpose entrusted to the letter.

On the very path before him, he beheld one named Kuraṅgaka approaching— a long-distance traveler without a specific destination, stumbling even on level ground due to his vacant heart; he was like a fragment of a dark rain-cloud portending a thunderbolt of evil tidings, like a sprout of smoke from the fire of grief about to blaze forth, and like the seed of a harvest of misfortune about to ripen.
Upon seeing him, his heart broke with fear, aroused by the succession of omens he had previously perceived.
Kuraṅgaka, however, having offered his salutations, approached; first he presented the dejection fixed upon his face, and afterwards the letter.
King Harṣa himself took it and read it.
Taking the very meaning of the letter to heart, he was overcome with grief and spoke in a choked voice:
"Kuraṅgaka, what is the illness of my father?
He replied simultaneously with eyes shedding tears and a mouth faltering with broken syllables: "Your Majesty, he has a great burning fever."
Upon hearing that, his heart suddenly split as if into a thousand pieces.

Having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth, and desiring long life for his father, he bestowed his entire personal wealth—an immeasurable collection of jewels, gold, and silver—upon the Brahmins.
Without even eating, he set forth.
And he spoke to a youth standing before him who was bearing a sword at his side, saying, "Have the horse's saddle prepared.
With a trembling heart, he mounted the steed brought by an attendant who had run forward in haste, and set out all alone.

Then, agitated by the sound of conchs signaling an untimely departure, the army—having been alerted in confusion and now surging forward—filled the entire hollow of the world with the loud clamor of its hooves as it arrived from every direction.
As he was galloping, this horse veered off its course.
And as he set forth, deer passing to his left signaled that destruction was at hand for the lion among kings.
Facing the orb of the hot-rayed sun, a crow perched upon wood dried by the forest fire and uttered a harsh cry, as if rending his very heart.

A naked mendicant, his body soiled by a thick layer of grime accumulated over many days as if made of lampblack, approached him with a crest of peacock feathers. His arrival was ill-omened and unwelcome; consequently, the king became deeply apprehensive. With a heart softened by affection for his father, he disregarded various portents while keeping his eyes fixed upon the shoulder of the horse.

Keeping his gaze steady and having brought his laughter and conversation to an end out of sorrow, he traversed a road spanning many *yojanas* in a single day, followed by the circle of kings who had fallen silent. As the divine sun, its luster vanished and its face turned downward as if dejected by the news of the king’s illness, [he was followed] by the circle of princes headed by Bhaṇḍi, who were full of affection.
Although he was being entreated, he took no food.
With the path cleared by a succession of villagers being led away by doorkeepers stationed in front, he was conducted through the night while still traveling.
On another day, at midday, the city was devoid of cries of victory, the sound of trumpets had ceased, singing had been withdrawn, and festivities were dispelled.

The city was devoid of the songs of wandering minstrels and the display of goods in the market stalls; in various places, it seemed to be scraped by the tips of the horns of Yama’s buffalo, as the rising streaks of smoke from the *koṭihoma* sacrifices— curved by the force of the wind— danced about, while it was being encircled by the snares of the noose of Kṛtānta,
and for a whole day, it resounded harshly with the tinkling of iron bells, like the ornaments on the buffalo of Time.
In one place, approaching misfortune was being signaled by circling flocks of crows; in another, a serpent-king (*ahirbudhnya*) was being propitiated by a grieving kinsman lying prostrate;

elsewhere, a circle of mothers was being pacified by a noble youth burning himself with torches; in another spot, the goddess Amardaka was being entreated by a Dravidian intent on offering a human head as a sacrifice; in yet another, Caṇḍikā was being beseeched by an Andhra who was raising his arms like a rampart; and in another place, Mahākāla was being conciliated by a new servant rendered helpless as the guggulu resin held upon his head was melting away.

In one place, groups of kinsmen were intent on performing *homa* sacrifices with their own flesh, severed by sharp knives; in another, the practice of selling human flesh was being carried out by the sons of illustrious kings.

It seemed as if it were struck by the dust of cremation grounds, seized by inauspicious omens, devastated by *yātudhānas*, swallowed by the age of Kali, covered by masses of sin, and plundered by the distractions of unrighteousness.
He reached the royal camp, which seemed as if overcome by the dominions of impermanence, appropriated by the play of destiny, empty, asleep, robbed, bewildered, deceived, and swooning.
Even as he entered, along the path of the marketplace, he saw [a scene] surrounded by a dense throng of children agitated by curiosity, with a large staff stretched out as a support.

He beheld a painted scroll of Yama, held in his left hand, which depicted the Lord of the Dead mounted upon a terrifying buffalo and accompanied by a ghost; on this scroll, he saw Yama narrating the events of the other world with an arrow-stalk held in his other hand.
And from that very scroll, he heard a verse being recited:
"Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, have passed away in age after age; to whom do they belong, or to whom do you belong?
With his heart being torn even more deeply by these words, he proceeded in due course toward the palace gate, where entry for all people had been forbidden.
Having dismounted from his horse, he saw a young physician named Suṣeṇa emerging from the inner apartments with a dejected facial expression, as if his senses were despondent.
After the youth had offered his salutations, he asked him:
"Suṣeṇa, is there any improvement in my father's condition, or not?"
He said: "If he were here now, I would see the prince.

Being greeted very slowly by the gatekeepers, he entered the place where all one's possessions were being offered, where the family deities were being worshipped, where the preparation of the *amṛta-caru* oblation had begun, where the six-fold *āhuti* sacrifice was being performed, and where trembling blades of *dūrvā* grass were being smeared with drops of *pṛṣadājya*.

The house was filled with the recitation of the Mahāmāyūrī, the performance of domestic propitiatory rites, and the offering of oblations for protection against malevolent spirits; it resounded with the chanting of the *Saṃhitā* by disciplined Brahmins and the sounds of the eleven-fold *Rudrīya* being muttered within the temple of Śiva; it witnessed the ritual bathing of the multi-eyed Lord Virūpākṣa with thousands of jars of milk prepared by exceedingly pure Śaivas; and it was crowded with those seated in the courtyard, their hearts distressed at not having obtained a sight of their master, who were receiving news from the attendants emerging from within.

Day and night were being passed by kings who, having abandoned all personal grooming through their reduced bathing, eating, and sleeping, appeared like figures in a painting due to their motionless state and soiled attire; meanwhile, on the thresholds, groups of men sat bound together, whispering—
some exposing the failings of physicians, some reciting the symptoms of incurable diseases, and others...

One person announced bad dreams; another disclosed news of demons; another revealed the predictions of fortune-tellers; one sang of omens; another meditated on impermanence and reviled cyclic existence;
another censured the play of the Kali age and reproached fate; yet another grew angry at dharma and insulted the tutelary deities of the royal house.
He entered the royal palace, where the wretched condition of the king was being described by an outer retinue who reproached the ill fortune of that afflicted young man of noble birth.

Being gazed upon by his father’s attendants, whose eyes were flooded with incessant tears, he reached the place while inhaling the scent of boiling decoctions, clarified butters, and oils— scented with various medicinal substances—
which were being cooked over a fire.

The third courtyard was there; it was exceedingly silent, guarded by many cane-bearers at the entrance of the house, with the paths of its fine walkways concealed by triple-layered curtains, its side doors closed, the rattling of its panels silenced, the air preserved within by latticed windows, and its attendants filled with distress.

In that place, the doorkeeper was enraged by the sound of footsteps striking the stairs; all activities were being signaled by silent gestures; the armored guards sat not too near; the water-bearer stood at a corner, startled by the summons; the circle of elders in the moon-chamber remained silent and hidden; the group of female relatives, distressed by great mental anguish, held their necks covered; and the anxious attendants were huddled together in the courtyard.

While a few trusted friends had entered [the palace], while the physicians were terrified by the onset of a deep-seated fever, while the ministers were despondent, while the family priest was faltering, while his friends were sinking, while the learned scholars were dispirited, while the devoted vassal kings were consumed with grief, while the attendants holding the fly-whisks were bewildered, while the head-protectors were emaciated by sorrow, while the wealth of his favors and the fulfillment of his subjects' desires were wasting away, and while his loyal vassals were weakened and deprived of strength because they had renounced food out of devotion to their lord; The output is: While a few trusted friends had entered [the palace], while the physicians were terrified by the onset of a deep-seated fever, while the ministers were despondent, while the family priest was faltering, while his friends were sinking, while the learned scholars were dispirited, while the devoted vassal kings were consumed with grief, while the attendants holding the fly-whisks were bewildered, while the head-protectors were emaciated by sorrow, while the wealth of his favors and the fulfillment of his subjects' desires were wasting away, and while his loyal vassals were weakened and deprived of strength because they had renounced food out of devotion to their lord;

In that place, where young princes who had remained awake throughout the entire night lay prostrate upon the surface of the earth; where a multitude of noble youths descended from ancient lineages bore aloft the pure bier;
where the joyful Nandin was shrunken with grief and devoid of delight; where the nearby attendants sighed in despair; where the women of the court had their lips grey with dried betel;

where the chamberlain was intent on gathering medicinal herbs as prescribed by the embarrassed physicians; and where the pain of parched mouths was being relieved by the streams of water from high goblets being drunk by the dependents.

In that place, where many gluttons were being fed according to the king’s desire; where all the merchants were busily engaged in procuring a complete assortment of medicinal ingredients; where the cooks were repeatedly summoned, their terrible thirst inferred from their condition;
where the water-jars were being cooled with snow; where the probes were made cool by camphor powder applied to white, damp cloths;
where fresh vessels were being smeared with un-dried mud for holding mouthfuls of liquid; and where soft lotus stalks were covered with the leaves of a moist, tender lotus-pond.

On the ground where water-basins were filled with clusters of blue lotuses together with their stalks, where boiled water was being cooled by the falling of streams, where the sharp scent of pink sugar was being released, where the inner eyes of water-jars resting on sandy beds were fixed upon the lattices, where the water-wheels were slipping as they were encircled by straight moss,

where coarse sugar was held in vessels that had drunk up the essence of parched grain flour made fragrant by the aroma of *galvarka* and *śālājīra*, and where heaps of crystal, mother-of-pearl, and conch shells were strewn with the powder of cooling medicinal juices.

He was staying in a white mansion where heaps of abundant, ancient, and fresh fruits—such as *āmalaka*, *mātuluṅga*, grapes, and pomegranates—were being presented to Brahmins, while drops of propitiatory water were being scattered; where female servants were applying medicinal pastes to the foreheads of the stone slabs; and where he sat upon a couch that was rippling with incessant tossing, as if being consecrated with the lustration-rite (*nīrājana*) by the fever-flame for victory over the next world, like the serpent Śeṣa in the Milky Ocean suffering from the heat of the poison.

He was struggling, whitened by the dust of pearl-sand like the ocean drying up at the time of cosmic destruction; he was being lifted up by Time, like Mount Kailāsa by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa; he was being touched by the white hands of female attendants intent on incessantly anointing him with sandalwood paste—hands that seemed to have been reduced to ash by the touch of his excessively hot limbs; and he was being bid farewell, under the guise of a sandalwood unguent, by his own enduring fame as it set out for the other world.

He bore a body variegated as if by the falling side-glances of Death, with its lotus, water-lily, and blue-lotus petals being incessantly plucked away; he carried a head from which the persistence of agonizing pain was made known by the hair at its edge being crushed by a thick silk cloth, and which was made terrifying by a network of dark veins rising due to unbearable agony, as if marking the number of days remaining until his death with lines drawn by the fingers of Time.

He inspired terror with his broad forehead and fixed his eyes— whose pupils had slightly retreated inward as if from the agitation of perceiving the approach of Yama— upon his face; he drew forth a succession of hot sighs like a mirage,

rippling with the grey rays emitted by his rows of parching teeth, while the onset of a dreadful fever was announced by his tongue, which was turning dark as if scorched by those excessively hot breaths.
With a jeweled necklace, pearls, sandalwood paste, and moonstones placed upon his chest, he made himself appear as if ready for the sight of the messengers of Death;

with his pair of arms raised by the twisting and stretching of his limbs, he seemed to construct a shower-house for the cooling of his heat by means of the rays from his outstretched fingernails falling upon the surfaces of the nearby water-jewels, the mosaic floors, and the mirrors. By means of these reflections falling there...

He seemed to be proclaiming an excess of internal torment as he touched his beloved, who was like a ground of trust; he held even fainting in high regard; he was possessed by omens of death perceived by fearful physicians as if they were the very syllables summoning the Ender;
at the time of his great departure, he was transferring the continuity of his own suffering into the hearts of his kinsmen, overcome by restlessness.

It was being abandoned by its shadow as if by envy; it was like an enterprise abandoned by calamities; it was made into a prisoner by exhaustion as if it were the discharge of all weapons; it was made an object of helplessness by agitation; it was made a field by adversity; it was made a range by decay; it was bitten by languor;
it was made one's own by ill-disposed sitting; it was brought under control by indisposition; and it was embraced by time through disease.
It was made its target by the southern quarter (the south), as if drunk by agonies, devoured by wakefulness, swallowed by pallor,
swallowed up by the breaking of limbs, carried away by calamities, partitioned by pains,
plundered by sorrows, sought to be seized by fate, determined by necessity, and smelled by impermanence.
Overcome by non-existence, conceived as dead, having granted an opening to the afflictions, he was a dwelling place for dejection;
near death, close to time, at the mouth of his final breath, at the gateway of the great departure, on the tip of the tongue of long sleep,
standing before the Lord of Life— scarcely audible in speech, agitated in mind, failing in body, yet abundant in [the approach of] the end of life.
He was constantly prattling and sighing, overcome by yawning fits; dependent on others and tormented by mental anxieties, he was pursued by recurring ailments.
And she sat beside him, her eyes swollen from incessant weeping, holding a fly-whisk yet fanning him only with her sighs;
her body greyed by the dust of various medicinal herbs, she cried out again and again, "Noble Lord, are you sleeping?"
He saw his father being touched on the head and chest by Queen Yaśomatī as she spoke.
Upon seeing this, his mind was tormented by the onset of his first sorrow, and he became as if apprehensive toward his fortunes;
he regarded his father as if already dwelling in the city of Death.
For a moment he was as if rejected by his own inner sense;

he was cast out by fortitude, made his domain by agitation, emptied by passion, and made an object of despondency. Bearing a heart as if composed of fire, and possessing senses that were fainting as if corrupted by poison, he seemed to sink into the underworld of darkness.
Even while distinguishing himself by his emptiness and surpassing even the sky, he found nothing further to be done;
yet he touched the earth with his heart and his head.

The lord of the earth, however, seeing his most beloved son from afar—even in that state—was overcome by intense affection; rushing forward in spirit, he stretched out his arms and called out, "Come, come!"
He rose from his bed with half his body;

and as he approached him in agitation, [the other] raised him up by force as he bowed low with humility, pressed him against his chest, and—entering, as it were, the center of the lunar orb through love; sinking, as it were, into a great lake of nectar; bathing him, as it were, in a vast [ocean].
As if being bathed by a stream of yellow sandalwood juice or by the melting waters of the snowy mountain, pressing limb against limb,

rubbing cheek against cheek, and closing his eyes which were dripping with a constant flow of tears matted at the tips of his lashes, he embraced her for a long time, forgetting the feverish torment of his illness.

Having somehow or other been released after a long time, he approached and sat down near the bed—having withdrawn, offered salutations, and bowed to his mother—and the king, as if drinking him in with an unwinking and motionless eye, touched him again and again with a hand trembling with emotion; then, his throat parched by exhaustion, he spoke with great difficulty:
"My child, you are thin."
Bhaṇḍi, however, said:
"Your Majesty, today is the third day since he has taken food.
Hearing this, his words choked by a surge of tears, he sighed deeply and somehow managed to speak: "My son, I know you to be dear to your father and possessed of an exceedingly tender heart."
In such circumstances, the exceedingly difficult-to-restrain affection for kinsmen, which overwhelms all, agitates the mind even of the wise; therefore,
you ought not to give yourself up to grief.

Though already consumed by the fever of a violent great burning, I am indeed burned even more intensely by this affliction of yours, O long-lived one. Your slenderness cuts me like a sharpened weapon.
My happiness, my kingdom, my lineage, my life, and my world beyond all rest upon you.
As it is for me, so it is for all subjects.
The afflictions of those such as you cause suffering to the entire surface of the world.
Persons like yourself do not adorn the lineage of those possessing little merit; this is the fruit of stainless karma accumulated over many previous births.

These marks of yours proclaim a sovereignty over even the four oceans as if it were held in the palm of your hand. By your very birth, I have achieved my life's purpose; I am now without desire for further existence.
"It is out of deference to the physician that he makes me drink this medicine.
Moreover, my child, parents are merely the means for those like you who are to be born for the sake of protecting the entire surface of the world through the merits of all living beings;
for kings have kinsmen in their subjects, not in their own blood relations."
"Therefore, arise.

Perform all your duties once again. And when you have finished eating, I too shall myself partake of wholesome food. When he was addressed in this way, the fire of grief, as if wishing to consume his very heart, blazed up even more intensely within him.

Having stood there for only a moment, he descended from the white palace as his father again commanded him to take food. And he reflected in his mind: "Truly, this great dissolution has arrived unexpectedly, like a thunderbolt falling from a cloudless sky. For even ordinary grief is death with breath still remaining; it is a great malady for which no medicine is prescribed, and it consumes one without reducing one to ashes."

Entering the fire is nothing but dwelling in hell for one who has not desisted; it is a rain of glowing coals, being cut into pieces, being sawn apart, and the falling of diamond needles upon one who is unwounded—
how much more so for one who relies on specific [faults]?
"What shall I do here? he thought.

And, directed by the king's officer, he went to his own home and took a few mouthfuls that were like smoke, causing tears to fall; like fire, producing a burning in the heart; like poison, inducing waves of fainting;
like great sins, engendering loathing; and like lye, bringing forth agonizing pain.
He also commanded his fly-whisk bearer to bring him mouth-washing water, saying,
"Go and find out how my father is doing.
Having gone and returned, the bearer reported, "Your Majesty, he is exactly as before," while the king himself, not yet having taken his betel, grew increasingly distressed.
When the sun had set, he summoned all the physicians to his presence and, with a despondent heart, asked them, "What should be done now for one in such a state?
They, however, replied, "O King, take courage."

"In just a few days, you will hear that your father has returned to his natural state and is restored to health. Now, among those physicians was a youth named Paunarvasu, about eighteen years of age, who had come to that very royal court through family succession; he had inherited the lineage of the eightfold Ayurveda and was cherished by the king no differently than his own son.
The young physician named Rasāyana, who by his very nature possessed an exceedingly sharp intellect and understood the true nature of diseases exactly as they were, stood with tears in his eyes,
silent and with his face cast downward.
When questioned by the prince, "Friend Rasāyana, tell me the truth regarding that which you perceive as being improper," he remained thus.
He said, "Your Majesty, tomorrow at dawn I shall report the matter exactly as it stands.
And in the meantime, the keeper of the palace lotus pond, consoling a *kokila* bird, recited aloud this *aparavaktra* verse:
"O bird, steady your mind; cast off your grief yourself and abide on the path of discernment."
The sun now rests upon the summit of Mount Sumeru together with the splendor of the lotus-lake.
Having heard that, Bāṇa, who was skilled in interpreting omens, utterly abandoned all hope for his father’s life.
When the physicians had departed, his fortitude shattered, he ascended once more toward the presence of the king at the onset of night.
And there, a great fever consumed him.
"Bring necklaces, O deer-eyed one! Place jeweled mirrors upon my body, O Vaidehī!
Anoint my forehead with flakes of snow, O playful lady!"
O fair-eyed one, apply the powder of camphor;
O radiant one, place a moonstone upon your eye; O lady of artistic grace, set a blue lotus upon your cheek.
"O Cārumatī, apply sandalwood paste;
O Pāṭalikā, fan the breeze with a cloth;
O Indumatī, alleviate the burning heat with lotuses; O Madirāvatī, produce joy with water-soaked [lotuses]; O [friend], bring the lotus stalks."
Mālatī, fan me with the palm-leaf; Āvantikā, bind my head that is reeling; Bandhumatī, support my neck;
Dhāraṇikā, hold me up; Kuraṅgavatī, place your hand with its spray of water upon my chest; Balāhikā, massage my arms;
Padmāvatī, press my feet; Anaṅgasenā, embrace me firmly; Vilāsavatī, what time is it?
"Sleep does not come; tell me a story, O night-lily!"—hearing such words from his father incessantly, with a grieving heart, he passed the night awake, which seemed long due to his sorrow.
At dawn, having descended, he went to his own quarters on foot, even though a horse had been brought by the groom approaching the palace gate.
Hurrying there for the sake of his brother’s arrival, he dispatched camel-herders who were swift-footed, capable of long journeys, and exceedingly fast, one after another.

Having washed his face, he did not accept the cosmetic preparations offered by his attendants. He heard the indistinct murmuring of "Rasāyana! Rasāyana! from the young princes standing before him, who were despondent.
And he questioned them, "Gentlemen, what is this elixir?
Being thus questioned, they all remained silent at once.
As he pressed them again and again, they spoke with great difficulty, "Your Majesty, he has entered the fire."
Upon hearing this, as if scorched within by a burning heat, he instantly turned pale.
His heart, blinded by grief, was unable to endure it, as if being torn asunder.

And the thought occurred to him: "It is true that one does not become [the cause of sorrow] oneself, yet a person of noble birth, unlike others, does not utter unpleasant or distressing words even when they must be told."

And he thought: "Just as this [fire] was practiced by him through hardship, it has been made to blaze up even more intensely by his entering the flames—like a noble youth of virtuous nature who is like refined gold.
Furthermore, he reflected: 'Or rather, this is entirely appropriate for one so full of affection.
Is his father not his father? Or is his mother not his mother? Are we not his brothers?'"

Even when any other master becomes difficult to find, lives being sustained in this world serve as a cause for modesty; how much more so in the case of my father, whose name is auspiciously invoked, who is composed of nectar, a sincere kinsman to his dependents, and whose favor is never barren?
At this moment, he has acted most appropriately by burning himself.
What indeed can be burned of him who remains unchanging, steadfast, and composed of glory?
He alone is fallen into the fire;
we, however, are the ones who are consumed.
Truly fortunate is that leader among the meritorious.

But this royal house is indeed devoid of merit, since it is bereft of such a noble son. Moreover, what burden of business, what remaining task, or what preoccupation do I have that my breaths of life, though cruel, do not yet depart?
"What obstacle is there in his heart that it does not shatter into a thousand pieces?
Thus afflicted by grief, he did not go to the royal palace;
he abandoned all his duties.
Having lain down upon his bed, he remained with his head and upper body covered by his upper garment.
And while King Harṣa was in such a state and the king himself remained in that condition, the hands of the entire world seemed nailed to their cheeks,
streams of tears were as if molded from clay upon their eyes, their gazes were as if knotted upon the tips of their noses, and [their sighs] were carved out upon their ears.

The sounds of weeping became as if innate to their tongues; the cries of "Alas, what misery! were as if sprouted upon their lips; the words of lamentation were as if inscribed upon their lower lips; and sorrows were as if stored away within their hearts.
Sleep, as if fearing the burning heat of hot tears, did not resort to the hollows of their eyes.
Her smiles vanished as if shaken away by the wind of her sighs;
her speech did not issue forth, as if entirely consumed by the heat of her anguish;
and even in her conversations, no jests were heard.
It was no longer known where the musical gatherings had gone;
the dances were not remembered, as if they belonged to another life;
and even in dreams, the ornaments were no longer grasped.
Even talk of enjoyments could not be obtained;
even the name of food was not mentioned.
The circles of drinking saloons became like flowers in the sky.
The words of the bards seemed to be brought from another world; the rites of cessation seemed to belong to another age;
and the god of love seemed to be consumed once more by the fire of grief.
Even by day, their beds were not released from sleep.
And gradually, great portents arose everywhere throughout the world, foreboding the downfall of the Great Man and instilling fear in all beings for the sake of the king’s demise.
For instance, the earth, with its entire circle of principal mountain ranges swaying, first trembled as if desiring to depart along with her lord.
In that interval, as if between the two Dhānvantaris, the oceans surged with waves made clamorous by their mutual clashing; they roiled like the seas at the end of an aeon.
To those terrified by the disappearance of the mountain-king (Himavat), comets rose up in all directions like masses of hair, formidable and curled with their outstretched crests of flame.
With the quarters of the sky made terrifying by these comets, the world became as if grey with the smoke from the *āyuṣkāma* oblations commenced by the guardians of the directions.

In the solar disc, which had lost its luster and was tawny like a vessel of molten iron, some being seeking the life of the king offered himself as a human sacrifice under the guise of a terrifying headless trunk.
The white-rayed moon appeared radiant with the full extent of its blazing halo, looking as if it had constructed a rampart of fire out of fear of the Rāhu who was yawning in his desire to seize it.
The quarters of the sky, won over by the majesty of the monarch, burned with passion as if they had already entered the flames.
The Earth, her body reddened by the showering spray of flowing blood, appeared as if she had donned a garment of pale-red silk to follow her husband in death.
The gates of the quarters were blocked by masses of untimely dark clouds, like iron door-panels brought forth by the world-protectors terrified by the sudden calamity of the king’s destruction.
The terrible, thunderous roars of falling thunderbolts swelled, sounding like the shrill blasts of kettledrums beaten for the departure of the Lord of the Dead, rending the very heart.
Showers of dust, tawny as the mane of a camel, turned the abode of the sun grey, as if raised by the hooves of Yama’s approaching buffalo.
Rows of jackals howled, seemingly receiving from the sky falling meteors, while their upward-turned faces and tongues of flame emitted a harsh, discordant cry.

In the capital city, the images of the family deities appeared as if manifesting grief through their disheveled locks of hair, their agitation revealed by the smoke swirling around the parts of their braided tresses.
A swarm of bees hovered in confusion near the throne, bearing the likeness of the matted locks of the Night of Doom being shaken by the wind;
for a moment, the cawing of the crows above the inner apartments did not cease.
From the center of the circle of the white parasol, a bird with a flickering beak and blood-red like a lump of fresh flesh seemed to snatch away the very life of the kingdom.
A cawing, aged vulture tore out a fragment of ruby from his high perch; tormented by this great ill omen, he passed the night with great difficulty.
On another day, from the royal palace, there approached him a woman whose ornaments jingled as they were shattered by her rapid pace.
She was made vocal by the tinkling of anklets moving upon her restless feet, as if with a cry of victory over despair, while she stood with necks upturned, asking: "What?"

As if being asked "What is this? by the palace swans from afar, who were making their voices ring out with the tinkling of their girdles as they stumbled over her broad hips; and as if being shown the way by the domestic cranes, who were blind with tears; she covered her face—which was like a piece of red silk torn by the impact against the closed door-panel—with a mass of blood from her forehead that had split open, and weeping, she let fall a stream of liquid from her golden bracelet that had melted under the force of her grief.

As if casting off a cane-stick, she let fall her upper garment— which was rippled by the wind from her face— quivering like a female serpent shedding its cluster of sloughs; and with her mass of hair, which was disheveled of its braided arrangement, dark blue as if made of *tamāla* shoots, swaying in the wind, and falling over her drooping shoulders, she covered her breasts, which were pained by the blow of her own chest.
Repeatedly shaking her sprout-like hands, whose palms were swollen, copper-colored, and dark, as if scorched by the constant wiping away of hot tears;

and bathing with the flickering rays of her pupils— set in motion by her darting eyes— the people standing near her who were reflected upon the surface of her cheeks as they dissolved in the waterfall of her gaze, making them appear darkened by her own sorrow as she seemed to immerse herself in the fire of grief.

As if burning even the day with her cries of "Where is the prince? Where is the prince? as she questioned every person she met, the female door-keeper named Velā arrived from the presence of Yaśomatī.
Greeted by the dejected eyes of the people as she approached, she placed both hands upon the mosaic floor, as if sprinkling it with the tears trickling down.
With her face cast downward, she addressed him whose dusty lower lip was drying with the streams of light from his teeth: "O King, save me! Save me!
What desperate act has the Queen resolved upon while her husband still lives?

Then, hearing those further words, he became paralyzed by uncertainty—seeming to lose his very being, as if melting away with grief, as if swallowed up by anxiety, as if weighed down by torment, and as if consumed by his own body.

And as he regained consciousness, this thought occurred repeatedly in his mind: "Though the onset of suffering falls upon my heart many times, it is like a blow from an iron mallet striking a hard stone; it rouses the fire within me, but it does not reduce the body of this pitiless man to ashes.
Having risen, he went quickly to the inner apartments.
And there, from afar, he heard the queens who were preparing to die: "O dear mango tree, think of yourself; your mother is departing on a journey.
O child, jasmine cluster, I am going; bid me farewell.
O sister, pomegranate vine of the palace, you will be without a protector today without me."

"O red Aśoka tree, forgive my kicks and the offense of breaking off your sprouts for ear-ornaments. My dear little Bālabakula of the inner apartments, you who are spoiled by receiving mouthfuls of wine, I have seen you.
My child Priyaṅgulatikā, embrace me tightly; I shall become difficult for you to attain."
"O auspicious one, you who assisted at the door of my house, let this handful of water for the funeral libation be given; you were my child.

O brother, parrot of the cage, speak what you have to say so that I may not forget you; I am far away from you, O maina. May our meeting again occur even in a dream. Mother, to whom shall I entrust the house-pheasant clinging to my path? O mother, this pair of swans must be cherished like a son; alas, I of meager merit did not foresee the loss of this pair of *cakravāka* birds."
O you who are affectionate toward your mother, turn back.
O fawn of the household, bring here the lute beloved by the chamberlains; let me embrace it for a moment.
Candrasenā, let this person be looked upon well.
Bindumatī, this is your final salutation.
Maid, release my feet.
Noble Kātyāyanikā, why do you weep? I have been carried away by fate.
Father Chamberlain, why do you circumambulate me, who am devoid of auspicious marks? Nurse, support yourself; why do you fall at my feet?
Sister, take me by the neck for the very last time! Alas, my dear friend Malayavati has not been seen!
O Kuraṅgavatī, this is my salutation with joined palms.
O Sānumatī, this is my final prostration. O Kuvalayavatī, this is my final embrace of you.
"Friends, these lovers' quarrels must be forgiven"—such were the conversations [he heard].
With his ears burning from them, as he was entering, he saw her coming out, having surrendered all her possessions and taken the ornaments for death;
she was like Jānakī about to enter the fire before her husband, appearing like the goddess Śrī with her body still moist from a recent bath.
She was like the Goddess [Lakṣmī] suddenly risen from the ocean, wearing two garments tawny as safflower that resembled the two splendors of twilight;
she bore upon her body a silk garment, red as a veil of light from the darkness of the betel-stained luster of her lower lip—
a mark of widowhood clinging to her limbs— and with a crimson neck-thread hanging between her breasts, she inspired the suspicion that it was a stream of blood trickling from a heart rent asunder.
She was constricting her neck with a pearl necklace whose strings were pulled by the sharp points of her earrings that were tilted askance; it appeared like a noose of white silk.

Because of the fresh saffron unguent on her body, she seemed as if swallowed by the blazing flames of a funeral pyre that desired to consume her, filling the lap of her garment with exceedingly white teardrops that resembled the flowers used for worshipping the fire of the pyre.
She seemed to scatter at every step with her slipping bracelets an offering to the household deities;

she wore a garland of flowers around her neck reaching down to her feet, as if she had mounted the swing of Yama’s realm; her lotus-eyes appeared to be addressed by the ear-lotus humming within it with bees;
and she was being circumambulated by her jeweled anklets, which moved in a circle like kinsmen.
She held motionless a picture-board, as dear to her as her own life, for the sake of death, like a swan in the lake of worldly existence;

she embraced her beloved royal parasol— white as her own pure conduct— as if it were a kinsman, while before it she shed tears from her eyes, like a banner of female devotion with white flower-garlands fluttering, bound to its staff, and raised toward her husband.

She was dismissing her ministers, who had with great difficulty accepted her command after she had restrained them with a flood of tears rising as they fell at their lord’s feet; she was being drawn by the cries from the household, which grew louder as the circle of distressed elderly kinsmen was turned back by her entreaties; and her heart was being carried away by the roars of the lions in their cages, which resembled the voice of her husband.
She was attended by her nurse with devotion to her husband, supported by her own fainting fit which had become chronic,
embraced by her friend who was accompanied by her own affliction, surrounded by her attendants whose every limb was seized by a consuming fever,
presided over by the elders who were sighing for the noble youth, and encompassed by chamberlains who were aged with sorrow.

He saw his mother following behind, shedding tears even for the dogs that were favorites of the king; falling at the feet of her co-wives; bidding farewell even to the painted dolls; offering salutations with joined palms even before the household birds; taking leave even of the domestic animals; and embracing even the trees of the palace grounds.

Even from afar, with eyes welling with tears, he cried out: "Mother, you too are abandoning me, whose merit is so meager! Be gracious; turn back! And even as he spoke these words, his crest being kissed, as it were, by the rays of the jewels in his anklets, Queen Yaśomatī stood there dejected before her younger and most beloved son, who had cast his head at her feet.
Held back by her teacher with a force like that of a mountain, as if entering the netherworld of the blinding darkness of a swoon,
and overwhelmed by a mass of affection that had long been pent up and now burst forth in a torrent of tears,
she was unable to prevent the flow of her tears despite her efforts to restrain them.

With the unbearable surge of grief made manifest by the violent trembling of her full breasts, her throat faltering as it was seized by a stammer, the region of her lower lip made to quiver by extraordinary indignation, her nostrils thickened by repeated throbbing, she closed her eyes and flooded her spotless cheeks with a flood of tears; then, covering them with the edge of her silken garment— which was inlaid with the rays of her fingernails and seemed like a stream of clear tears emerging from within her body— she wept.

With her moon-like face slightly upturned and her heart tormented, she— her breasts flowing with milk— recollected his entire childhood as he lay in her lap from the day of his birth; her heart fixed upon the house of her kinsmen,
she cried out again and again to her parents, "O Mother, O Father, do not look upon me, a sinner who has departed for the next world and am thus exceedingly distressed!"

"Alas, my child! You have not been seen by me, whose fortune has come to rest"—thus lamenting for her eldest and most beloved son who was absent; "I have become protectorless"—thus grieving for her daughter residing in her father-in-law's house; "O merciless one, what offense has this person committed against you?"—thus reproaching fate; and "There is no woman equal to me in the sharing of sorrow."

Censuring herself in many ways, she cried out for a very long time with a loud voice like an ordinary woman: "I am robbed! O cruel Kṛtānta, I have been ruined by you! Thus she reviled Kṛtānta unexpectedly.
When the force of her grief had subsided, she affectionately raised up her son.
With his hand, he wiped away the prince’s weeping eyes, whose gaze flowed more copiously as if liquefied by the mass of teardrops gathered upon the lashes.

He himself, meanwhile, had eyes distressed by the continuous falling of a succession of exceedingly fine teardrops; their pupils were starred with white spray, and their inner corners—being released from the whiteness swallowed up by intense passion—were overflowing at the edges with boiling tears.

Again and again, as her face was being filled with tears, she wiped away the tresses of hair hanging down from her cheeks— tresses held fast by cheeks moist with weeping and reaching to the tips of her ears— and pushed aside the mass of locks that lay askew, disheveled by the loose, dangling curls falling below;
then, lifting with her hand the upper garment over her breast, which was wet and somewhat displaced, filled with a stream of tears and rippled, as it were, by the web of light from her fingernails.

Having washed her lotus-face with water poured from the beak of a silver royal swan— a vessel for her beauty, marked by a thin copper streak at the edge of her magnificent silken garment— and having wiped her hands clean upon two pure pieces of cloth held by the silent and mute attendants, she stood for a long time with her pair of eyes fixed intently on her son’s face; then, sighing deeply again and again, she spoke:
My child, there is no one so dear to me, nor anyone devoid of virtue, nor anyone worthy of abandonment. My very heart was drunk along with your milk.
Yet, at this moment, my sight, obstructed by the abundant favor of my lord, does not behold you.
Moreover, my son, I am neither the goddess Lakṣmī, who is addicted to gazing upon other men, nor am I Kṣamā, who is devoid of compassion;
I am the wife of a noble house, whose only wealth is her character, born into a family pure in its dharma.
Have you forgotten me, the wife of that preeminent man—who was like a lion, renowned for his prowess in a hundred battles—just as one forgets a lioness?
How could one like me, born of a hero, the wife of a hero, and the mother of a hero—purchased by the price of valor—act otherwise?
By such a father as yours, resembling Bharata, Bhagīratha, and Nābhāga, a bull among the hosts of kings, was your hand taken.
And with your head, you have received the consecration from golden jars offered by the wives of endless vassal lords, who were agitated in their service.
My forehead has obtained the honor of the binding of the Great Queen’s diadem, a fulfillment of desires difficult to attain.
My breasts have been suckled by sons such as you, while they wear Chinese silks fluttering in the breeze of the yak-tail whisks fanned by throngs of enemies’ wives and female captives.
And my pair of feet has been placed upon the heads of rival queens, honored by the rows of rubies in the crowns of all the wives of the bowing courtiers.
Thus, with all my limbs having achieved their purpose, what else do I require? My merit exhausted, I desire only to die while still a widow.
Yet, I cannot utter useless lamentations like those of a woman bereft of her noble husband, now that my own lord has been consumed by fire.
Furthermore, like the dust from your father’s feet, I shall be highly esteemed by the celestial nymphs who are devoted to heroes as I announce my first journey to the heavens.
And for me, already consumed by the harsh suffering I have just witnessed, what more will the fire have left to burn? At this moment, life itself would be a rash act compared to death.
This fire is far more intense than the fire of grief for my husband, fueled as it is by the inexhaustible fuel of my love.

While the Lord of Life dwells upon Mount Kailāsa, how can greed for a life as insignificant as a blade of withered grass even be conceivable? Moreover, O son, the joys of your kingdom will not touch me, for I am a great sinner who disregarded the king while he was still living.
Furthermore, for those consumed by grief, prosperity becomes inauspicious, ill-omened, useless, and devoid of purpose.

"My child, I wish to remain in this world through the fame of those who trust me, not through my physical form. Therefore, my dear, I myself shall first seek your favor; I must no longer be tormented by the frustration of my desires.
Having said this, she fell at her feet.
He, however, hurriedly withdrew his feet and, with his body bowed low, raised his mother—who held her form with both hands and had her head touching the ground.

Perceiving the inevitability of her grief and considering that very action to be the most meritorious, as it was appropriate for a woman of noble family, he remained silent with his face cast down, knowing her resolve.
For even in those distressed by affection, a sense of noble breeding accords with the requirements of place and time.

Queen Yaśomatī also embraced him and, having smelled the crown of his head, departed from the inner apartments on foot; as if obstructed by the quarters of the sky filled with the echoes of the citizens' lamentations, she went to the bank of the Sarasvatī.
There, with glances timid by the nature of women, she worshipped the fire Citrabhānu as if with clusters of blooming red lotuses, just as the lunar form might worship the divine sun.

The other, too, overwhelmed by the death of his mother and surrounded by a circle of kinsmen, went to his father’s side. There he beheld his progenitor, whose vital functions were reduced to a mere remnant, with his pupils rolling, like the king of stars (the moon) desiring to set. And, assailed by an unbearable surge of grief, he was robbed of his fortitude by affection.

Embracing his lotus-feet—which were caressed by the garlands of crowns of all the haughty kings—he beheld a continuous stream of clear tears flowing from his eyes like a great cloud; it was as if the internal heat were melting away from his moon-like face, as if a mass of moonlight from his teeth were turning to water, as if the beauty of his eyes were dissolving, and as if the nectar-essence of his face were trickling down. His eyes were like a great rain-cloud.
Showering as it were with tears and emitting a continuous cry, he wept for a long time.
But the king, his vision obstructed by those [tears] and his hearing occupied by the incessant sound of weeping, recognized him and spoke very slowly:
"My son, you ought not to be thus."
For those like you are not lacking in great courage;
indeed, it is great courage that is the primary support for the world, and only thereafter does royal splendor follow.

Where are you—the foremost among the courageous, relying on every excellence—and where is this despondency? To say "you are a lamp of your lineage" is like diminishing one whose brilliance is equal to the sun.
"To say 'You are a lion among men' is like an insult to one whose valor is augmented by heroism and sharp wisdom.

To say 'This earth is yours' is like a redundancy for one whose status as a universal monarch is proclaimed by his physical marks. To say 'Accept this fortune' is like a contradiction for one who has already been embraced by Fortune herself."
"To occupy this world" seemed like an insufficient goal to one who desired to conquer both worlds;
"let the treasury be accepted" seemed useless to one whose sole devotion was to the accumulation of fame as pure as the rays of the moon;
and "let the circle of kings be made one's own" seemed redundant to one who had already made the entire world his own through his multitude of virtues.

"To let the burden of the kingdom be carried [by another]" was like an improper separation for one accustomed to bearing the weight of the three worlds; "to protect the subjects" was like a mere restatement for one whose long, staff-like arms had already seized the quarters of the horizon;
"to look after the retinue" was like a secondary consequence for one who resembled a world-protector.
What more need be commanded of one whose forearm is blackened by the calluses of constant practice with the bow?
"The host of your restlessness must be restrained"—this is a command that finds no scope for my words in one who has already subdued his senses at such a tender age.
"The enemies must be brought to total destruction"—this is a concern that belongs only to your innate splendor.
Speaking thus, the lion among kings closed his eyes so that they would never open again, and the son of Pūṣan (Yama) took possession of him.

In that very interval, Pūṣan himself was deprived of both his life and his splendor; and thereafter, as if feeling ashamed of the offense against his own son born from taking away the king’s life, he became downcast with his face turned downward.
Scorched within by the fire of grief for the loss of the protector of the earth, he attained a coppery hue.
Descending from heaven very slowly, as if complying with worldly custom for the sake of an unpleasant inquiry,
he approached the vicinity of the western ocean as if wishing to offer a handful of water to the lord of men.
Having immediately offered that handful of water, his thousand hands turned blood-red, as if scorched by the fire of grief.
And so, as the sun—its vast body appearing tranquil as if through the immense world-weariness born of the death of the great lord of men—entered the depths of a mountain cave;

as the day turned blue, as if scorched by the heat of the many hot sighs of men and drenched as if by the rainy clouds of tears shed by the multitude, while the world grew red as if from the glow of the eyes of all people turning crimson with weeping, and the sunlight was extinguished; Thus ends the passage.

As the lotus beds were being abandoned by Lakṣmī, who seemed to have set out in pursuit of the king; as the earth grew dark, its luster withdrawn as if out of grief for her husband; as the distressed ruddy geese, like noble kinsmen who had forsaken their wives, took refuge in the forest depths after uttering piteous cries; and as the day-lotuses closed their buds in concealment, as if terrified of the collapse of the royal umbrella.

When the crimson glow had faded— like a flood of blood from the hearts of the quarters, those brides now rent asunder— and when the Lord of Light had gradually departed for the other world, leaving behind only his passion;
and when twilight had set in, pale-red with a thick hue spreading across the expanse of the sky like the banner of the Lord of the Dead.
While streaks of darkness— repulsive to the sight and quivering like black yak-tail fans adorning a funeral bier— were spreading across the night,
which had become as dark as black aloe-wood and appeared as if a pyre had been constructed by some unknown hand;
and while the splendors of the night-lotuses, their ear-petals adorned with ivory-white beauty and their heads wreathed with filaments, stood with smiling faces as if prepared to die along with him.

While the moon was appearing in the eastern quarter— heard as if echoing the tinkling of the bells of the celestial chariots descending, and filled with the warbling of flocks of birds nesting upon the treetops like the royal parasol being met by Indra for a king setting out on the path to heaven— the lord of men, equal to Śibi, took up the bier himself along with his vassals who had offered their shoulders.
The citizens, led by the family priest, escorted her to the river Sarasvatī and, upon a funeral pyre befitting a sovereign,
reduced her to a state where only her fame remained through the rites of the sacrificial fire.
King Harṣa, too, was accompanied by the entire circle of the royal household, as if by the whole world of living beings gathered together in one place.

Surrounded by a silence born of grief, though inwardly consumed by the fire of sorrow and as if being drenched from within by the melting flow of affection, he sat upon the bare earth and remained awake throughout that entire night, as fearsome as the river Bhīmarathī, together with the king.
And this thought arose in his mind: "Now that my father has passed away, this world of the living has indeed become so small; all its hopes are shattered."

The paths of desires have become barren; the seats of prosperity have been blocked; the gates of bliss are closed; truthfulness has fallen asleep; the conduct of worldly life has vanished; the possession of great arms has dissolved; sweet speech has disappeared; the playful variations of manly prowess have gone abroad;
pride in battle has reached its end; delight in the virtues of others has been destroyed; the grounds of trust have come to rest; and noble deeds have ceased to exist.

Treatises have become useless; valor, being without support, remains as a mere subject of discourse; discernment bids farewell with a final libation of water; let the people embrace renunciation in place of vigor; let sovereignty over subjects adopt the single braid of widowhood;
let noble humanity take refuge in a hermitage; and let the Earth don two white garments in place of royal splendor.

Let elegance wear bark garments; let majesty perform penance in the groves of asceticism; let heroism clothe itself in rags. Where, then, can gratitude go for his sake? And where will the Supreme Creator ever again find such atoms for the creation of great men? The ten directions have become empty of virtues; the world has become shrouded in darkness; and the Dharma has become fruitless.

Now, what kind of birth is this for those who subsist by the sword? Without my father, how could there be such assemblies of heroes—days whose talk of strife, commenced with the passion of unequalled battle, pricks the cheeks of the brave warriors?

Would that his lotus-face, with its long red eyes, might be seen again even in a dream; and would that I might embrace him once more, even in another life, he whose massiveness exceeds that of a pillar of iron!
"Even in another world, may her voice—deep as the surging of the churned Ocean of Milk and pouring forth nectar—be heard again and again as she addresses him, 'O son!
As he reflected on these and other such thoughts, the night somehow came to an end.
Then, as flocks of cocks began to crow aloud with cries of grief, as if letting out a loud lament, and were causing themselves to fall from the peaks of houses, mountains, and trees...
At the hour of dawn, when the peacocks had abandoned their temple-dwellings, when the winged birds had set out for the forest leaving their own homes,
when the darkness— now thinned and fading away— was languishing, when the lamps, their self-love diminished, were longing for extinction,
and when the sky, its body clothed in the bark-garment of shimmering crimson rays, had as if entered the life of a wandering mendicant; [The sun arose.]
As the stars, grey as the necks of sparrows, were being submerged like fragments of a king’s bones;
as herds of wild elephants set out toward various lakes, rivers, and sacred bathing-places, bearing jars filled with the earth’s essence;
and as the moon, pale as a mass of fresh, pure beeswax, was being cast down upon the shore of the western ocean like a funeral ball of rice.

And gradually, as the host of stars set, the king’s splendor seemed to grow dim as if by the spreading smoke from the funeral pyre of the monarch; his heart seemed darkened by the soot of the scorching rays of the fire of grief for the lord of men; his body seemed withered by the agitation caused by the moon-like faces of all the women of the inner apartments who had departed; and his mind seemed despondent through the longing for Rohiṇī, who had first vanished—just as the sun ascended to heaven when the kingdom itself had undergone a transformation.
At the close of night, King Harṣa set out for his bath like a bed of lotuses awakened by the circle of roused royal swans;
meanwhile, in the inner apartments, the palace swans were silenced by the cessation of the sound of anklets and the harem was reduced to only a few chamberlains overwhelmed with grief,
while the attendants of his father stood in the inner courtyards like a herd of wild elephants whose leader has fallen, plunged in despair.

With his gaze fixed upon the royal elephant, which lay panting and motionless as it sat atop its pillar, and upon the royal horse, which stood in the courtyard and was being signaled by the cries of the stable-keepers, and amidst the great assembly hall that had become empty and silent save for the lingering echoes of the shouts of victory, he departed from the palace with eyes burning with anguish.
And he went to the bank of the Sarasvatī.
Having bathed in it, he offered water for his father.
Having performed the ritual ablution, yet without wringing out his hair, he put on two fresh garments of fine silk; then, intent on sighing, he proceeded without an umbrella.
Remaining motionless even when the horse was brought before him, he gazed with his feet alone, his eyes— red as blood-lotuses and fixed upon the tip of his nose—

seeming to vomit forth the fire of grief out of fear for the cremation of his father who now remained only in his heart; and by the luster of his lower lip, which was naturally pale-red like a sprout of the Kalpavriksha tree, tender as a fresh leaf and untouched by betel yet long washed clean, he seemed to swallow mouthfuls of flesh and blood.

As if vomiting forth hot sighs from the very blow to his heart, he returned to the palace. On that very day, however, the king’s favorites, servants, friends, and ministers departed; abandoning their beloved children and wives, though restrained by their tearful kinsmen, they—whose hearts were captivated by the multitude of the king’s virtues—some [abandoned] themselves.

Some among the Bhṛgus bound themselves [to vows]; some remained right there at the sacred fords; others, with their minds distressed and having spread out grass and *kuśa* blades, quelled their incomparable grief through fasting; some, helpless under the impulse of sorrow, entered the fire like moths; and others, their hearts burning with the fire of terrible suffering, took refuge with the Mountain of Snow, having taken a vow of silence.

Some went to the valleys of the Vindhya mountains, where their bodies were sprinkled by the spray from the trunks of herds of wild elephants; reclining on beds of young shoots, they allayed their fever.

Others, having abandoned even the objects of sense that were close at hand, turned away from service and took possession of the empty forest lands with limited alms. Some, subsisting on air alone and possessing the wealth of righteousness, blew upon their bellows.
Some became sages who, donning saffron robes, studied the doctrine of Kapila on the mountains; others, having made Śiva their refuge, grew matted locks upon heads where crest-jewels had been removed.
Others, clothed in long, pale-red monastic garments, displayed a brilliant devotion to their Lord.
Some reached old age with their bodies being licked by the tips of the tongues of the deer in the penance groves;
others, however, having taken vows, wandered about shaven-headed, carrying water in water-pots and with eye-sockets of deep coppery hue wiped by their sprout-like hands.
Even King Harṣa was in such a state, overwhelmed by grief for his father, regarding prosperity as a curse and the earth as a great sin.
Thus, he regarded sovereignty as a disease, enjoyments as serpents, his home as hell, kin as bondage,
life as infamy, the body as treachery, health as a stain, longevity as the fruit of demerit, food as poison,
poison as nectar, sandalwood as fire, desire as a saw, and [worldly existence] as the rending of the heart.

And seeing him thinking thus, regarding worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and turning his face away from all ritual activities—[he was addressed by] long-standing noble sons descended from the lineages of his father and grandfather; teachers whose words were to be accepted due to the respect instilled by their ancestral succession;

aged twice-born ones (*jaraddvijāti*) expert in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Itihāsa*; ministers and kings endowed with learning, noble birth, and good character; and those who had correctly realized the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*).

And they surrounded him— well-known wandering mendicants, sages who shared equally in sorrow and joy, experts in explaining the worthlessness of cyclic existence, exponents of the Veda, and masters of the Purāṇas skilled in dispelling grief.
Rendered dependent by them, he was unable even in his mind to indulge in the inclination toward sorrow.
Being entreated by his many friends and kinsmen, he with great difficulty turned his attention toward such activities as taking food;
yet, with his heart fixed on his brother, he thought:
"Perhaps, having heard of my father’s death—which is like the great dissolution of the world—the noble one, bathed in tears, might not take up the bark garments."
Or the royal sage might not resort to a hermitage; or that lion among men might not enter a mountain cave;
or, with his pair of lotus-eyes filled to overflowing with tears, he might behold the protectorless earth.
Or, overwhelmed by the harshness of his first calamity, Puruṣottama might remember his true self;
or, having developed detachment through the realization of impermanence, he might not reject the approaching royal fortune;
or, his body aflame with the fire of terrible suffering, he might undergo the consecration.

"Having come here, even when addressed by kings, one should not behave with discourtesy. Indeed, my noble brother is excessively partial toward his father; he always addresses me with praise for my father, saying, "Dear Harṣa, has there ever been anyone such as you before, or will there ever be again?"
This body is as tall as a golden palm tree; this great lotus-face is turned upward and blossomed throughout the day out of affection for the sun;

these two arms are as radiant as pillars of diamond; and these graceful gestures possess the charm of the *haladhara* [Balarāma], languid with laughter and wine. Who else could be so proud, so valiant, or so generous?
Reflecting on these and other matters, his heart longing for a sight [of his brother], he remained there with great difficulty, awaiting his brother’s arrival.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Death of the Great King," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the great poet Śrī Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
